newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. TREASURIES EXTEND LOSSES IN TOKYO BEFORE DATA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. TREASURIES EXTEND LOSSES IN TOKYO BEFORE DATA.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries continued their downward march by Tokyo midday on Wednesday due to follow-through selling, traders said.
The market carried over a downward trend from late New York trade, with operators aggressively looking for chances to unload their long positions on rallies.
"There is continuing nervousness about tonight's retail sales," a U.S. brokerage manger said.
"That nervousness was reinforced by last night's Johnson Redbook figures, which were again very strong."
The Redbook report was up by 0.9 percent in the first week of August with most retailers saying sales were better than planned.
U.S. brokerages were detected selling T-bond futures contracts this morning ahead of a series of U.S. indicators, with interest particularly on retail sales.
Economists forecasted retail sales data to show a rise of 0.7 percent in July after rising 0.5 percent in June.
Falls in the futures market dragged down cash prices, with the key 6-5/8 percent 30-year bond falling to 95-30/32, yielding 6.69 percent, from 96-5/32 in New York on Tuesday.

"There's a good chance the market will target a yield (for the 30-year bond) of about 6.75 percent in the near term, depending on the results of the retail sales data today," a Japanese brokerage trader said.
Dealers said sentiment turned even weaker after the September T-bond futures contract fell below a key technical support of 112-8/32 this morning.
"Downward pressure seems to have intensified even more this morning. Looking at the falls in the T-bond futures market, the market is pretty eager about selling," the Japanese brokerage trader said.
At midday, the September T-bond futures contract was at around 112-3/32 compared to the previous close of 112-15/32. It was moving in a range of 112-2/32 to 112-14/32.
Traders said Japanese investors could show buying interest in the shorter-end of the market, but that they are unlikely to buy aggressively as the dollar is not seen rising sharply against the yen.

"With the yield of two-year notes above six percent, Japanese investors may show some interest, but they could be a bit nervous due to unclear trend in the U.S. stock market and the dollar," the Japanese brokerage trader said.
